**Public Health Region 1 – Texas DSHS offices (excluding the headquarters in Lubbock)**  

| City | DSHS Office Location | Address & Phone |
|------|----------------------|-----------------|
| Amarillo | Regional Sub‑Office | 3407 Pony Express Way, Amarillo, TX 79118 – Phone 806‑655‑7151 |
| Hereford | Regional Field Office | 600 N 25 Mile Ave Ste 500, Hereford, TX 79045 – Phone 806‑364‑4579 |
| Pampa | Regional Field Office | 121 S Gillespie St, Pampa, TX 79065 – Phone 806‑665‑1690 |
| Dumas | Regional Field Office | 501 Success Blvd, Dumas, TX 79029 – Phone 806‑421‑0316 |

**Sources**

1. *Immunizations* page – “Our Regional Office is in Lubbock, our Regional Sub‑Office is in Amarillo, and our Regional Field Offices are in Hereford, Pampa, and Dumas.”【*source*】  
2. *Public Health Region 1 Clinics* page – lists the same locations with addresses and phone numbers for each city【*source*】.  

These are the DSHS offices within Public Health Region 1 other than the main headquarters in Lubbock.

From the headquarters in Austin to eligibility offices in the Rio Grande Valley to laboratories in the Panhandle, Health and Human Services employees are there to respond to the needs of Texans.
If you are deaf, hard of hearing, or speech impaired you can call any Texas Health and Human Services office by using the relay service of your choice. The state of Texas offers Relay Texas which you can use by dialing 7-1-1 or 800-735-2989.

## Main Headquarters
Texas Health and Human Services are headquartered in Austin, Texas. If you need to contact someone at one of the main offices, also called state office headquarters, please use the addresses and phone numbers below.
Health and Human Services  
Texas Health and Human Services (HHS) state office headquarters is located at:
North Austin Complex
4601 W. Guadalupe St.
Austin, TX 78751-3146
P.O. Box 13247
Austin, Texas 78711-3247
Main number: 512-424-6500
TTY number: 512-424-6597
Media calls: 512-424-6951
Texas Department of State Health Services
The Texas Department of State Health Services state office headquarters is located at:
1100 West 49th St.
Austin, Texas 78756-3199
P.O. Box 149347
Austin, Texas 78714-9347
Other DSHS contact information.

## HHS Offices
Offices and Service Providers
*   Aging and Disability Resource Centers (ADRC) contract with HHS to provide information to Texans who are older or who have disabilities so they can find the right long-term care services. You also can call **855-937-2372**.  
*   Area Agencies on Aging (AAA) contract with HHS to provide local services to anyone 60 and older and their caregivers. You also can call **800-252-9240**.  
*   Community Services Regional Offices provide administrative support to community services contractors and enroll people in community services programs.  
*   DSHS Locations includes contact information for the health services regions, community mental health centers, public health organizations, and state hospitals.  
*   Local Intellectual and Developmental Disability Authorities contract with HHS to provide services to people who have intellectual and developmental disabilities.  
*   Long-term care services – Use this search to find long-term care regional offices, area agencies on aging, local intellectual and developmental disability authorities, and aging and disability resource centers.  
*   Regulatory Services Regional Offices provide administrative support to Regulatory Services staff in the regions.  
*   Rehabilitation Services Offices – Use this search to find your nearest rehabilitation services office.  
*   Service and Benefits Offices provides a searchable list of benefit offices around the state.  
*   State Supported Living Centers provide campus-based direct services and supports to people with intellectual and developmental disabilities at 13 locations around the state.
Ombudsman Offices

texts.0:
From the headquarters in Austin to eligibility offices in the Rio Grande Valley to laboratories in the Panhandle, Health and Human Services employees are there to respond to the needs of Texans.
If you are deaf, hard of hearing, or speech impaired you can call any Texas Health and Human Services office by using the relay service of your choice. The state of Texas offers Relay Texas which you can use by dialing 7-1-1 or 800-735-2989.
texts.1:
## Main Headquarters
Texas Health and Human Services are headquartered in Austin, Texas. If you need to contact someone at one of the main offices, also called state office headquarters, please use the addresses and phone numbers below.
Health and Human Services  
Texas Health and Human Services (HHS) state office headquarters is located at:
North Austin Complex
4601 W. Guadalupe St.
Austin, TX 78751-3146
P.O. Box 13247
Austin, Texas 78711-3247
Main number: 512-424-6500
TTY number: 512-424-6597

Texas Department of State Health Services
The Texas Department of State Health Services state office headquarters is located at:
1100 West 49th St.
Austin, Texas 78756-3199
P.O. Box 149347
Austin, Texas 78714-9347
Other DSHS contact information.
texts.2:
## HHS Offices
Offices and Service Providers
*   Aging and Disability Resource Centers (ADRC) contract with HHS to provide information to Texans who are older or who have disabilities so they can find the right long-term care services. You also can call **855-937-2372**.  
*   Area Agencies on Aging (AAA) contract with HHS to provide local services to anyone 60 and older and their caregivers. You also can call **800-252-9240**.  
*   Community Services Regional Offices provide administrative support to community services contractors and enroll people in community services programs.  
*   DSHS Locations includes contact information for the health services regions, community mental health centers, public health organizations, and state hospitals.  
*   Local Intellectual and Developmental Disability Authorities contract with HHS to provide services to people who have intellectual and developmental disabilities.  
*   Long-term care services – Use this search to find long-term care regional offices, area agencies on aging, local intellectual and developmental disability authorities, and aging and disability resource centers.  
*   Regulatory Services Regional Offices provide administrative support to Regulatory Services staff in the regions.  
*   Rehabilitation Services Offices – Use this search to find your nearest rehabilitation services office.  
*   Service and Benefits Offices provides a searchable list of benefit offices around the state.  
*   State Supported Living Centers provide campus-based direct services and supports to people with intellectual and developmental disabilities at 13 locations around the state.
Ombudsman Offices

Region 1 includes many counties: Armstrong, Bailey, Briscoe, Carson, Castro, Childress... etc. The public health region likely covers 31 counties. The regional office might be located in Lubbock? Wait Region 1 is the Panhandle region? Actually the Texas DSHS health region 1 might be "North Texas"? Let's search.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Texas Department of State Health Services  
DSHS Headquarters in Austin, Texas  
Agency overview  
Formed 2003  
Preceding agencies*   Texas Department of Health
*   Texas Department of Mental Health and Mental Retardation  
*   Texas Health Care Information Council  
*   Texas Commission on Alcohol and Drug Abuse  
JurisdictionTexas  
Headquarters*   Austin, Texas  
Agency executives*   Imelda Garcia, Interim Comissioner  
*   Rachel Hendrickson, Head of Staff  
*   Kim White, Senior Advisor  
Parent agencyTexas Health and Human Services Commission
Austin State Hospital
**Texas Department of State Health Services** is a state agency of Texas. The department was created by House Bill 2292 of the 78th Texas Legislature in 2003 through the merging of four state agencies: the Texas Department of Health, Texas Department of Mental Health and Mental Retardation, Texas Health Care Information Council, and Texas Commission on Alcohol and Drug Abuse.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-1) The department provides state-operated health care services, including hospitals, health centers, and health agencies. The agency is headquartered at the Central Campus at 1100 West 49th Street in Austin.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-2) The DSHS Council governs the department.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-3)

The agency's Mental Health and Substance Abuse Division, along with Public Policy Research Institute at Texas A&M University coordinate the Texas School Survey,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-4) a program consisting of two surveys on drug and alcohol abuse, an annual one done at the local school-district level and a biennial statewide survey. The statewide survey, called the Texas School Survey of Substance Use, is the largest survey of its kind to be conducted in the United States and administered to over 100,000 public school students between grades 7–12.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-6)
Dr. Jennifer Shuford is the Commissioner of the Texas Department of State Health Services. She was appointed to this position in December 2022.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-7)

## Geographic structure
[edit]
The agency provides an array of public health services and oversight across the state through eight regional offices.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-10)
*   Region 1 - Lubbock  
*   Region 2/3 - Arlington  
*   Region 4/5 North - Tyler  
*   Region 6/5 South - Houston  
*   Region 7 - Temple  
*   Region 8 - San Antonio  
*   Region 9/10 - El Paso  
*   Region 11 - Harlingen

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Texas Department of State Health Services  
DSHS Headquarters in Austin, Texas  
Agency overview  
Formed 2003  
Preceding agencies*   Texas Department of Health
*   Texas Department of Mental Health and Mental Retardation  
*   Texas Health Care Information Council  
*   Texas Commission on Alcohol and Drug Abuse  
JurisdictionTexas  
Headquarters*   Austin, Texas  
Agency executives*   Imelda Garcia, Interim Comissioner  
*   Rachel Hendrickson, Head of Staff  
*   Kim White, Senior Advisor  
Parent agencyTexas Health and Human Services Commission
Austin State Hospital
**Texas Department of State Health Services** is a state agency of Texas. The department was created by House Bill 2292 of the 78th Texas Legislature in 2003 through the merging of four state agencies: the Texas Department of Health, Texas Department of Mental Health and Mental Retardation, Texas Health Care Information Council, and Texas Commission on Alcohol and Drug Abuse.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-1) The department provides state-operated health care services, including hospitals, health centers, and health agencies. The agency is headquartered at the Central Campus at 1100 West 49th Street in Austin.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-2) The DSHS Council governs the department.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-3)
texts.1:
The agency's Mental Health and Substance Abuse Division, along with Public Policy Research Institute at Texas A&M University coordinate the Texas School Survey,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-4) a program consisting of two surveys on drug and alcohol abuse, an annual one done at the local school-district level and a biennial statewide survey. The statewide survey, called the Texas School Survey of Substance Use, is the largest survey of its kind to be conducted in the United States and administered to over 100,000 public school students between grades 7–12.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-6)
Dr. Jennifer Shuford is the Commissioner of the Texas Department of State Health Services. She was appointed to this position in December 2022.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-7)
texts.2:
## Geographic structure
[edit]
The agency provides an array of public health services and oversight across the state through eight regional offices.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-10)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Texas Department of State Health Services  
DSHS Headquarters in Austin, Texas  
Agency overview  
Formed 2003  
Preceding agencies*   Texas Department of Health
*   Texas Department of Mental Health and Mental Retardation  
*   Texas Health Care Information Council  
*   Texas Commission on Alcohol and Drug Abuse  
JurisdictionTexas  
Headquarters*   Austin, Texas  
Agency executives*   Imelda Garcia, Interim Comissioner  
*   Rachel Hendrickson, Head of Staff  
*   Kim White, Senior Advisor  
Parent agencyTexas Health and Human Services Commission
Austin State Hospital
**Texas Department of State Health Services** is a state agency of Texas. The department was created by House Bill 2292 of the 78th Texas Legislature in 2003 through the merging of four state agencies: the Texas Department of Health, Texas Department of Mental Health and Mental Retardation, Texas Health Care Information Council, and Texas Commission on Alcohol and Drug Abuse.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-1) The department provides state-operated health care services, including hospitals, health centers, and health agencies. The agency is headquartered at the Central Campus at 1100 West 49th Street in Austin.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-2) The DSHS Council governs the department.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-3)

The agency's Mental Health and Substance Abuse Division, along with Public Policy Research Institute at Texas A&M University coordinate the Texas School Survey,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-4) a program consisting of two surveys on drug and alcohol abuse, an annual one done at the local school-district level and a biennial statewide survey. The statewide survey, called the Texas School Survey of Substance Use, is the largest survey of its kind to be conducted in the United States and administered to over 100,000 public school students between grades 7–12.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-6)
Dr. Jennifer Shuford is the Commissioner of the Texas Department of State Health Services. She was appointed to this position in December 2022.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-7)

## Geographic structure
[edit]
The agency provides an array of public health services and oversight across the state through eight regional offices.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-10)
*   Region 1 - Lubbock  
*   Region 2/3 - Arlington  
*   Region 4/5 North - Tyler  
*   Region 6/5 South - Houston  
*   Region 7 - Temple  
*   Region 8 - San Antonio  
*   Region 9/10 - El Paso  
*   Region 11 - Harlingen

The PHR 1 Immunization Program provides services to 44 counties in the Texas Panhandle and South Plains. Our Regional Office is in Lubbock, our Regional Sub-Office is in Amarillo, and our Regional Field Offices are in Hereford, Pampa, and Dumas. We also work with theLocal Health Departmentsin the region.
The mission of the Immunization Division is to improve the quality and longevity of life for people in Texas by achieving and maintaining a vaccine-preventable disease-free environment. This will add to the state's economic base by avoiding substantial healthcare costs. This mission will be achieved through the utilization of cost-effective immunization programs and efficient epidemiology applied in quality partnerships with public and private participants (local, state, and national) who share the common vision of community well-being.
For Immunization Program-related questions, contact [Marie Hernandez, RN](mailto:MarieD.Hernandez@dshs.texas.gov), Immunization Program Supervisor for PHR 1.
Refer to the DSHS Immunization website for ImmTrac2, IQIP, and Texas Vaccine for Children (TVFC).

The PHR 1 Immunization Program provides services to 44 counties in the Texas Panhandle and South Plains. Our Regional Office is in Lubbock, our Regional Sub-Office is in Amarillo, and our Regional Field Offices are in Hereford, Pampa, and Dumas. We also work with theLocal Health Departmentsin the region.
The mission of the Immunization Division is to improve the quality and longevity of life for people in Texas by achieving and maintaining a vaccine-preventable disease-free environment. This will add to the state's economic base by avoiding substantial healthcare costs. This mission will be achieved through the utilization of cost-effective immunization programs and efficient epidemiology applied in quality partnerships with public and private participants (local, state, and national) who share the common vision of community well-being.
For Immunization Program-related questions, contact [Marie Hernandez, RN](mailto:MarieD.Hernandez@dshs.texas.gov), Immunization Program Supervisor for PHR 1.
Refer to the DSHS Immunization website for ImmTrac2, IQIP, and Texas Vaccine for Children (TVFC).

Markdown Content:

## [PDF page 1]
Removing vaccine access barriers  
by hosting on-farm vaccine clinics for  
dairy workers and their families
Community-Based Promising Practice  
In March 2020, dairy workers were deemed essential workers and continued working throughout  
the COVID-19 pandemic. As COVID-19 vaccines became available in 2021, Dr. Anabel Rodriguez,  
an Assistant Professor of Epidemiology at University of Texas School of Public Health (UTSPH),  
and the Texas Department of State Health Services (DSHS) Public Health Region 1, partnered to  
remove vaccine access barriers by hosting on-dairy farm vaccine clinics for dairy workers and  
their  families.  This  collaborative  work  helped  bridge  relationships  between  local  health  
departments, dairy producers, and dairy workers in the lower portion of the Texas Panhandle, the  
South Plains region of Texas.
Partners:  
University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston School of Public Health in San Antonio  
https://sph.uth.edu/research/centers/swcoeh/dairy-farm-safety/  
Aurora Organic Dairy: https://www.auroraorganic.com/  
Two dairy farms in Stratford and Dublin, TX  
Texas Department of State Health Services (DSHS) Public Health Region 1  
https://www.dshs.texas.gov/region1/default.shtm  
Location: Stratford and Dublin, TX
Description of the Practice:  
Starting March 31, 2021, Dr. Anabel Rodriguez’s UT Health team and volunteer interpreters  
facilitated on-dairy farm COVID-19 vaccine clinics by bridging established relationships with  
Texas Department of State Health Services (DSHS) Public Health Region 1 in Lubbock, Texas,  
and  Aurora Organic Dairy  in  Stratford  and  Dublin,  Texas.  Dr.  Rodriguez’s  and  her  team’s  
farmworker research and outreach efforts and pre-existing relationships with producers in this  
rural  region  of  Texas  helped  propel  this  initiative  into  action.  This  multi-agency  vaccine  
collaboration created an open line of communication between the public health offices in the  
Texas Panhandle and the dairy farm leadership, dairy farm workers, and their families.
PDF link  
PDF link  
PDF link  
PDF link

## [PDF page 2]
Key Strategies:  
At the dairy cafeteria, Dr. Rodriguez and her graduate research assistant Sofia N. Lopez provided  
COVID-19 vaccine education sessions to dairy workers in English and Spanish and COVID-19  
vaccine FAQs videos in K’iche’, an Indigenous language spoken in Guatemala. Most of the dairy  
workers are of Mexican descent in the Panhandle, but this area has experienced an increase in  
K’iche’ peoples from Guatemala and H-2A guest workers. They offered sessions to groups of  
workers with space for one-on-one conversations between work shifts one week before the on-  
site vaccination clinics with Texas DSHS and their mobile unit.
This  COVID-19  vaccine  initiative  required  coordination  from  the  Aurora  Organic  Dairy  
management to promote sessions by circulating flyers created by their team, talking to the dairy  
supervisors,  and  sending  critical  Spanish  text  messages  to  dairy  workers  through  a  
communication platform often used by health clinics. Although some workers speak K’iche’, the  
dairy management asked bilingual dairy workers to interpret the text promotions to K’iche’  
workers. The dairy also offered workers incentives of $50 per vaccine dose.
Dr. Rodriguez and the UTSPH team’s goal was to host as many on-dairy farm vaccine clinics and  
vaccinate as many dairy workers as possible. Their schedule changed every day depending on the  
availability of vaccines and the availability of Texas DSHS staff (scheduled out-of-office clinics  
Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Fridays from either 10:00 am -3:00 pm or split days on smaller farms  
9:30 am-noon and 1:30 pm -4:00 pm). DSHS’s clinical staff consisted of Melanie Lee, RN  
(Clinical manager/director), four Texas DSHS registered nurses, four contract LVNs through the  
state of Texas, and six onsite data entry people from Lubbock, TX.
Dr. Carol Howe of Texas Christian University  
vaccinating dairy farm employee on April 30, 2021
PDF link

## [PDF page 3]
Results:  
According to Aurora Organic Dairy management, reaching 50% vaccination coverage among  
employees at the two locations was easy, but getting 50% to 70% was difficult and getting 70%  
to 90% was extremely difficult. The team helped Aurora Organic Dairy reach 99% vaccination  
coverage among  the  165  dairy  employees  in Stratford and Dublin, Texas  by addressing  
vaccination hesitancy and misinformation and providing on-site access to vaccines.
On April 6, 2021, the team administered 48 J&J vaccines to dairy workers in Stratford, TX.  
From April 30, 2021 – June 11, 2021, the team administered the Moderna vaccine to dairy  
workers: 11 received the first dose and 11 received the second dose. This collaborative effort  
took four on-site vaccine clinics.
Dr. Rodriguez and her team continue to partner with Aurora Organic Dairy beyond the on-  
site COVID-19 vaccine clinics. Her team recently delivered bovine tuberculosis education to  
118 employees in Stratford, TX.
Key Challenges and How They Were Addressed:  
COVID-19 Vaccine Hesitancy and Misinformation  
To combat COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy and misinformation, Dr. Anabel Rodriguez and Dr. David  
Douphrate created a series of COVID-19 vaccine Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)  interview  
videos with two Houston-based medical doctors in English, Spanish, and K’iche’. Through a  
project funded by USDA-NIFA's Agriculture and Food Research initiative, they created trainings  
about  COVID-19  transmission  and  prevention,  COVID-19  vaccine,  tuberculosis,  bovine  
tuberculosis, and  influenza and  the  flu  vaccine  on  mobile  tablet  devices. Their  team also  
contracted a Guatemalan teacher to translate and record K’iche’ audio. In uploading educational  
trainings to offline compatible tablet devices, dairy workers used disposable headphones as an  
asynchronous personal mobile-learning experience in English, Spanish, or K’iche’. This feature  
allowed workers to receive education on their own schedule, within a certain timeframe.
PDF link  
PDF link  
PDF link

## [PDF page 4]
In addition to the mobile learning, the team also scheduled dairy worker health and safety training,  
including vaccine education, a week before facilitating on-dairy farm COVID-19 vaccine clinics with Texas  
DSHS. The additional education leading up to the clinic date allowed dairy workers and their family  
members enough time and space, after vaccine education, to make a choice for their health.
Anabel Rodriguez (UTSPHYour paragraph text) delivering COVID-19 vaccine education to  
dairy farm employees on April 29, 2021.  
Language Barriers  
The Spanish language barrier was also a key challenge in the on-site vaccination clinics. DSHS and Dr.  
Rodriguez’s team provided general vaccine education in Spanish in group settings on the day of the  
vaccinations and provided one-on-one interpretation for individuals who had personal questions about  
vaccinations.The on-site interpreters helped promote trust, allay fears, and encourage compliance among  
dairy workers. With this model, dairy workers can develop questions and communicate concerns about the  
COVID-19 vaccine and receive answers to their questions.
PDF link

## [PDF page 5]
Maximizing dairy farmworkers’ time  
Texas DSHS staff provided the following vaccines to dairy farm workers at the onsite clinics:  
COVID-19,  Tdap,  MMR,  and  influenza.  Local  community  partners  provided  the  following  
resources, and education materials for dairy workers during the 15-minute observation period  
post-vaccine:  
Resources: Face masks, first aid kits, water bottles, and hand sanitizers, long sleeve work  
shirts, and hygiene kits  
Types of education: English language services, legal aid information, primary care referrals  
and information for migratory workers and families, heat stress prevention and safety,  
families in crisis information, immigration assistance, turberculosis awareness, education, and  
contact information, sexually transmitted disease information and education, health services  
offered to women and children, afterschool programs and school lunch programs.
When dairy farm workers’ time is restricted, or their work is a priority, it is important to give  
information and community resources that are meaningful and beneficial while they are there  
during the 15-30 waiting periods. If the clinic was supplying a two-dose vaccine, the dairy farm  
workers also received information about when to get the second dose of their COVID-19  
vaccines.
Transportation for family members  
All family members of the dairy farm workers, including non-employees, were invited to the  
onsite COVID-19 vaccination clinics. Family members who were unable to get vaccinated during  
these events due to a lack of transportation or conflicting work schedules got connected with  
trusted local representatives to receive the COVID-19 vaccine in their community. They also  
received follow-up services from the Migrant Education Program and Family Support Services.
PDF link

## [PDF page 6]
Resources Needed and Expenses:  
Aurora Organic Dairyoffered dairy workers $50 per vaccine dose to achieve high vaccination  
rates among staff. If a worker received a J&J/Janssen primary series, they received $50, and if a  
worker received a two shot primary series, Moderna or Pfizer, they received a total of $100. Dairy  
leadership required persistency in its efforts to promote vaccination clinics through flyers,  
meeting announcements, and Spanish text messages. If a worker had side effects from the  
vaccine, they could take the day off with pay and without any questions from dairy management.
Dr. Anabel Rodriguez and Dr. Douphrate of UTSPH provided culturally sensitive and linguistically  
appropriate COVID-19 education in paper flyers and audio pieces (English, Spanish, K’iche’).  
Through United Stated Department of Agriculture (USDA) funding, their research team created  
COVID-19 mitigation and prevention educational materials for dairy workers.
Twenty iPad tablets were available to dairy workers to create an asynchronous personal mobile-  
learning  experience  in  English,  Spanish,  or  K’iche’.  Funding  from  the  National  Center  for  
Farmworker Health (NCFH)Demonstration Grantalso supported their efforts to vaccinate dairy  
farm workers and their families.
Texas  DSHS  Public  Health  Region‘s  team  consisted  of  Melanie  Lee,  RN  (Clinical  
manager/director), four Texas DSHS registered nurses, four contract LVNs through the state of  
Texas, and six onsite data entry people from Lubbock, TX to help with consents and forms. The  
Preparedness and Response (PAR)team helped set up tarps and chairs, and Public Health Region  
1 Immunization Programassured all COVID-19 vaccines, Tdap, MMR, and influenza vaccines were  
onsite. Each onsite vaccination event required 22-23 individuals, including multiple volunteer  
interpreters/translators and individuals from local partnership organizations.
Partners:  
· Migrant Education Program (MEP)Region 16  
· Family Support Servicesin Amarillo, TX  
·Texas RioGrande Legal Aid

## [PDF page 1]
Removing vaccine access barriers  
by hosting on-farm vaccine clinics for  
dairy workers and their families
Community-Based Promising Practice  
In March 2020, dairy workers were deemed essential workers and continued working throughout  
the COVID-19 pandemic. As COVID-19 vaccines became available in 2021, Dr. Anabel Rodriguez,  
an Assistant Professor of Epidemiology at University of Texas School of Public Health (UTSPH),  
and the Texas Department of State Health Services (DSHS) Public Health Region 1, partnered to  
remove vaccine access barriers by hosting on-dairy farm vaccine clinics for dairy workers and  
their  families.  This  collaborative  work  helped  bridge  relationships  between  local  health  
departments, dairy producers, and dairy workers in the lower portion of the Texas Panhandle, the  
South Plains region of Texas.
Partners:  
University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston School of Public Health in San Antonio  
https://sph.uth.edu/research/centers/swcoeh/dairy-farm-safety/  
Aurora Organic Dairy: https://www.auroraorganic.com/  
Two dairy farms in Stratford and Dublin, TX  
Texas Department of State Health Services (DSHS) Public Health Region 1  
https://www.dshs.texas.gov/region1/default.shtm  
Location: Stratford and Dublin, TX
Description of the Practice:  
Starting March 31, 2021, Dr. Anabel Rodriguez’s UT Health team and volunteer interpreters  
facilitated on-dairy farm COVID-19 vaccine clinics by bridging established relationships with  
Texas Department of State Health Services (DSHS) Public Health Region 1 in Lubbock, Texas,  
and  Aurora Organic Dairy  in  Stratford  and  Dublin,  Texas.  Dr.  Rodriguez’s  and  her  team’s  
farmworker research and outreach efforts and pre-existing relationships with producers in this  
rural  region  of  Texas  helped  propel  this  initiative  into  action.  This  multi-agency  vaccine  
collaboration created an open line of communication between the public health offices in the  
Texas Panhandle and the dairy farm leadership, dairy farm workers, and their families.

PDF link  
PDF link

texts.2:
## [PDF page 2]
Key Strategies:  
At the dairy cafeteria, Dr. Rodriguez and her graduate research assistant Sofia N. Lopez provided  
COVID-19 vaccine education sessions to dairy workers in English and Spanish and COVID-19  
vaccine FAQs videos in K’iche’, an Indigenous language spoken in Guatemala. Most of the dairy  
workers are of Mexican descent in the Panhandle, but this area has experienced an increase in  
K’iche’ peoples from Guatemala and H-2A guest workers. They offered sessions to groups of  
workers with space for one-on-one conversations between work shifts one week before the on-  
site vaccination clinics with Texas DSHS and their mobile unit.
This  COVID-19  vaccine  initiative  required  coordination  from  the  Aurora  Organic  Dairy  
management to promote sessions by circulating flyers created by their team, talking to the dairy  
supervisors,  and  sending  critical  Spanish  text  messages  to  dairy  workers  through  a  
communication platform often used by health clinics. Although some workers speak K’iche’, the  
dairy management asked bilingual dairy workers to interpret the text promotions to K’iche’  
workers. The dairy also offered workers incentives of $50 per vaccine dose.
Dr. Rodriguez and the UTSPH team’s goal was to host as many on-dairy farm vaccine clinics and  
vaccinate as many dairy workers as possible. Their schedule changed every day depending on the  
availability of vaccines and the availability of Texas DSHS staff (scheduled out-of-office clinics  
Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Fridays from either 10:00 am -3:00 pm or split days on smaller farms  
9:30 am-noon and 1:30 pm -4:00 pm). DSHS’s clinical staff consisted of Melanie Lee, RN  
(Clinical manager/director), four Texas DSHS registered nurses, four contract LVNs through the  
state of Texas, and six onsite data entry people from Lubbock, TX.
Dr. Carol Howe of Texas Christian University  
vaccinating dairy farm employee on April 30, 2021
PDF link
texts.3:
## [PDF page 3]
Results:  
According to Aurora Organic Dairy management, reaching 50% vaccination coverage among  
employees at the two locations was easy, but getting 50% to 70% was difficult and getting 70%  
to 90% was extremely difficult. The team helped Aurora Organic Dairy reach 99% vaccination  
coverage among  the  165  dairy  employees  in Stratford and Dublin, Texas  by addressing  
vaccination hesitancy and misinformation and providing on-site access to vaccines.
On April 6, 2021, the team administered 48 J&J vaccines to dairy workers in Stratford, TX.  
From April 30, 2021 – June 11, 2021, the team administered the Moderna vaccine to dairy  
workers: 11 received the first dose and 11 received the second dose. This collaborative effort  
took four on-site vaccine clinics.
Dr. Rodriguez and her team continue to partner with Aurora Organic Dairy beyond the on-  
site COVID-19 vaccine clinics. Her team recently delivered bovine tuberculosis education to  
118 employees in Stratford, TX.
Key Challenges and How They Were Addressed:  
COVID-19 Vaccine Hesitancy and Misinformation  
To combat COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy and misinformation, Dr. Anabel Rodriguez and Dr. David  
Douphrate created a series of COVID-19 vaccine Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)  interview  
videos with two Houston-based medical doctors in English, Spanish, and K’iche’. Through a  
project funded by USDA-NIFA's Agriculture and Food Research initiative, they created trainings  
about  COVID-19  transmission  and  prevention,  COVID-19  vaccine,  tuberculosis,  bovine  
tuberculosis, and  influenza and  the  flu  vaccine  on  mobile  tablet  devices. Their  team also  
contracted a Guatemalan teacher to translate and record K’iche’ audio. In uploading educational  
trainings to offline compatible tablet devices, dairy workers used disposable headphones as an  
asynchronous personal mobile-learning experience in English, Spanish, or K’iche’. This feature  
allowed workers to receive education on their own schedule, within a certain timeframe.

PDF link  
PDF link
texts.4:
## [PDF page 4]
In addition to the mobile learning, the team also scheduled dairy worker health and safety training,  
including vaccine education, a week before facilitating on-dairy farm COVID-19 vaccine clinics with Texas  
DSHS. The additional education leading up to the clinic date allowed dairy workers and their family  
members enough time and space, after vaccine education, to make a choice for their health.
Anabel Rodriguez (UTSPHYour paragraph text) delivering COVID-19 vaccine education to  
dairy farm employees on April 29, 2021.  
Language Barriers  
The Spanish language barrier was also a key challenge in the on-site vaccination clinics. DSHS and Dr.  
Rodriguez’s team provided general vaccine education in Spanish in group settings on the day of the  
vaccinations and provided one-on-one interpretation for individuals who had personal questions about  
vaccinations.The on-site interpreters helped promote trust, allay fears, and encourage compliance among  
dairy workers. With this model, dairy workers can develop questions and communicate concerns about the  
COVID-19 vaccine and receive answers to their questions.
PDF link
texts.5:
## [PDF page 5]
Maximizing dairy farmworkers’ time  
Texas DSHS staff provided the following vaccines to dairy farm workers at the onsite clinics:  
COVID-19,  Tdap,  MMR,  and  influenza.  Local  community  partners  provided  the  following  
resources, and education materials for dairy workers during the 15-minute observation period  
post-vaccine:  
Resources: Face masks, first aid kits, water bottles, and hand sanitizers, long sleeve work  
shirts, and hygiene kits  
Types of education: English language services, legal aid information, primary care referrals  
and information for migratory workers and families, heat stress prevention and safety,  
families in crisis information, immigration assistance, turberculosis awareness, education, and  
contact information, sexually transmitted disease information and education, health services  
offered to women and children, afterschool programs and school lunch programs.
When dairy farm workers’ time is restricted, or their work is a priority, it is important to give  
information and community resources that are meaningful and beneficial while they are there  
during the 15-30 waiting periods. If the clinic was supplying a two-dose vaccine, the dairy farm  
workers also received information about when to get the second dose of their COVID-19  
vaccines.
Transportation for family members  
All family members of the dairy farm workers, including non-employees, were invited to the  
onsite COVID-19 vaccination clinics. Family members who were unable to get vaccinated during  
these events due to a lack of transportation or conflicting work schedules got connected with  
trusted local representatives to receive the COVID-19 vaccine in their community. They also  
received follow-up services from the Migrant Education Program and Family Support Services.
PDF link
texts.6:
## [PDF page 6]
Resources Needed and Expenses:  
Aurora Organic Dairyoffered dairy workers $50 per vaccine dose to achieve high vaccination  
rates among staff. If a worker received a J&J/Janssen primary series, they received $50, and if a  
worker received a two shot primary series, Moderna or Pfizer, they received a total of $100. Dairy  
leadership required persistency in its efforts to promote vaccination clinics through flyers,  
meeting announcements, and Spanish text messages. If a worker had side effects from the  
vaccine, they could take the day off with pay and without any questions from dairy management.
Dr. Anabel Rodriguez and Dr. Douphrate of UTSPH provided culturally sensitive and linguistically  
appropriate COVID-19 education in paper flyers and audio pieces (English, Spanish, K’iche’).  
Through United Stated Department of Agriculture (USDA) funding, their research team created  
COVID-19 mitigation and prevention educational materials for dairy workers.
Twenty iPad tablets were available to dairy workers to create an asynchronous personal mobile-  
learning  experience  in  English,  Spanish,  or  K’iche’.  Funding  from  the  National  Center  for  
Farmworker Health (NCFH)Demonstration Grantalso supported their efforts to vaccinate dairy  
farm workers and their families.
Texas  DSHS  Public  Health  Region‘s  team  consisted  of  Melanie  Lee,  RN  (Clinical  
manager/director), four Texas DSHS registered nurses, four contract LVNs through the state of  
Texas, and six onsite data entry people from Lubbock, TX to help with consents and forms. The  
Preparedness and Response (PAR)team helped set up tarps and chairs, and Public Health Region  
1 Immunization Programassured all COVID-19 vaccines, Tdap, MMR, and influenza vaccines were  
onsite. Each onsite vaccination event required 22-23 individuals, including multiple volunteer  
interpreters/translators and individuals from local partnership organizations.

· Family Support Servicesin Amarillo, TX  
·Texas RioGrande Legal Aid

an Assistant Professor of Epidemiology at University of Texas School of Public Health (UTSPH),  
and the Texas Department of State Health Services (DSHS) Public Health Region 1, partnered to  
remove vaccine access barriers by hosting on-dairy farm vaccine clinics for dairy workers and  
their  families.  This  collaborative  work  helped  bridge  relationships  between  local  health  
departments, dairy producers, and dairy workers in the lower portion of the Texas Panhandle, the  
South Plains region of Texas.
Partners:  
University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston School of Public Health in San Antonio  
https://sph.uth.edu/research/centers/swcoeh/dairy-farm-safety/  
Aurora Organic Dairy: https://www.auroraorganic.com/  
Two dairy farms in Stratford and Dublin, TX  
Texas Department of State Health Services (DSHS) Public Health Region 1  
https://www.dshs.texas.gov/region1/default.shtm  
Location: Stratford and Dublin, TX
Description of the Practice:  
Starting March 31, 2021, Dr. Anabel Rodriguez’s UT Health team and volunteer interpreters  
facilitated on-dairy farm COVID-19 vaccine clinics by bridging established relationships with  
Texas Department of State Health Services (DSHS) Public Health Region 1 in Lubbock, Texas,  
and  Aurora Organic Dairy  in  Stratford  and  Dublin,  Texas.  Dr.  Rodriguez’s  and  her  team’s  
farmworker research and outreach efforts and pre-existing relationships with producers in this  
rural  region  of  Texas  helped  propel  this  initiative  into  action.  This  multi-agency  vaccine  
collaboration created an open line of communication between the public health offices in the  
Texas Panhandle and the dairy farm leadership, dairy farm workers, and their families.
PDF link  
PDF link  
PDF link  
PDF link

## [PDF page 2]
Key Strategies:  
At the dairy cafeteria, Dr. Rodriguez and her graduate research assistant Sofia N. Lopez provided  
COVID-19 vaccine education sessions to dairy workers in English and Spanish and COVID-19  
vaccine FAQs videos in K’iche’, an Indigenous language spoken in Guatemala. Most of the dairy  
workers are of Mexican descent in the Panhandle, but this area has experienced an increase in  
K’iche’ peoples from Guatemala and H-2A guest workers. They offered sessions to groups of  
workers with space for one-on-one conversations between work shifts one week before the on-  
site vaccination clinics with Texas DSHS and their mobile unit.
This  COVID-19  vaccine  initiative  required  coordination  from  the  Aurora  Organic  Dairy  
management to promote sessions by circulating flyers created by their team, talking to the dairy  
supervisors,  and  sending  critical  Spanish  text  messages  to  dairy  workers  through  a  
communication platform often used by health clinics. Although some workers speak K’iche’, the  
dairy management asked bilingual dairy workers to interpret the text promotions to K’iche’  
workers. The dairy also offered workers incentives of $50 per vaccine dose.
Dr. Rodriguez and the UTSPH team’s goal was to host as many on-dairy farm vaccine clinics and  
vaccinate as many dairy workers as possible. Their schedule changed every day depending on the  
availability of vaccines and the availability of Texas DSHS staff (scheduled out-of-office clinics  
Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Fridays from either 10:00 am -3:00 pm or split days on smaller farms  
9:30 am-noon and 1:30 pm -4:00 pm). DSHS’s clinical staff consisted of Melanie Lee, RN  
(Clinical manager/director), four Texas DSHS registered nurses, four contract LVNs through the  
state of Texas, and six onsite data entry people from Lubbock, TX.
Dr. Carol Howe of Texas Christian University  
vaccinating dairy farm employee on April 30, 2021
PDF link

## [PDF page 3]
Results:  
According to Aurora Organic Dairy management, reaching 50% vaccination coverage among  
employees at the two locations was easy, but getting 50% to 70% was difficult and getting 70%  
to 90% was extremely difficult. The team helped Aurora Organic Dairy reach 99% vaccination  
coverage among  the  165  dairy  employees  in Stratford and Dublin, Texas  by addressing  
vaccination hesitancy and misinformation and providing on-site access to vaccines.
On April 6, 2021, the team administered 48 J&J vaccines to dairy workers in Stratford, TX.  
From April 30, 2021 – June 11, 2021, the team administered the Moderna vaccine to dairy  
workers: 11 received the first dose and 11 received the second dose. This collaborative effort  
took four on-site vaccine clinics.
Dr. Rodriguez and her team continue to partner with Aurora Organic Dairy beyond the on-  
site COVID-19 vaccine clinics. Her team recently delivered bovine tuberculosis education to  
118 employees in Stratford, TX.
Key Challenges and How They Were Addressed:  
COVID-19 Vaccine Hesitancy and Misinformation  
To combat COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy and misinformation, Dr. Anabel Rodriguez and Dr. David  
Douphrate created a series of COVID-19 vaccine Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)  interview  
videos with two Houston-based medical doctors in English, Spanish, and K’iche’. Through a  
project funded by USDA-NIFA's Agriculture and Food Research initiative, they created trainings  
about  COVID-19  transmission  and  prevention,  COVID-19  vaccine,  tuberculosis,  bovine  
tuberculosis, and  influenza and  the  flu  vaccine  on  mobile  tablet  devices. Their  team also  
contracted a Guatemalan teacher to translate and record K’iche’ audio. In uploading educational  
trainings to offline compatible tablet devices, dairy workers used disposable headphones as an  
asynchronous personal mobile-learning experience in English, Spanish, or K’iche’. This feature  
allowed workers to receive education on their own schedule, within a certain timeframe.
PDF link  
PDF link  
PDF link

## [PDF page 4]
In addition to the mobile learning, the team also scheduled dairy worker health and safety training,  
including vaccine education, a week before facilitating on-dairy farm COVID-19 vaccine clinics with Texas  
DSHS. The additional education leading up to the clinic date allowed dairy workers and their family  
members enough time and space, after vaccine education, to make a choice for their health.
Anabel Rodriguez (UTSPHYour paragraph text) delivering COVID-19 vaccine education to  
dairy farm employees on April 29, 2021.  
Language Barriers  
The Spanish language barrier was also a key challenge in the on-site vaccination clinics. DSHS and Dr.  
Rodriguez’s team provided general vaccine education in Spanish in group settings on the day of the  
vaccinations and provided one-on-one interpretation for individuals who had personal questions about  
vaccinations.The on-site interpreters helped promote trust, allay fears, and encourage compliance among  
dairy workers. With this model, dairy workers can develop questions and communicate concerns about the  
COVID-19 vaccine and receive answers to their questions.
PDF link

## [PDF page 5]
Maximizing dairy farmworkers’ time  
Texas DSHS staff provided the following vaccines to dairy farm workers at the onsite clinics:  
COVID-19,  Tdap,  MMR,  and  influenza.  Local  community  partners  provided  the  following  
resources, and education materials for dairy workers during the 15-minute observation period  
post-vaccine:  
Resources: Face masks, first aid kits, water bottles, and hand sanitizers, long sleeve work  
shirts, and hygiene kits  
Types of education: English language services, legal aid information, primary care referrals  
and information for migratory workers and families, heat stress prevention and safety,  
families in crisis information, immigration assistance, turberculosis awareness, education, and  
contact information, sexually transmitted disease information and education, health services  
offered to women and children, afterschool programs and school lunch programs.
When dairy farm workers’ time is restricted, or their work is a priority, it is important to give  
information and community resources that are meaningful and beneficial while they are there  
during the 15-30 waiting periods. If the clinic was supplying a two-dose vaccine, the dairy farm  
workers also received information about when to get the second dose of their COVID-19  
vaccines.
Transportation for family members  
All family members of the dairy farm workers, including non-employees, were invited to the  
onsite COVID-19 vaccination clinics. Family members who were unable to get vaccinated during  
these events due to a lack of transportation or conflicting work schedules got connected with  
trusted local representatives to receive the COVID-19 vaccine in their community. They also  
received follow-up services from the Migrant Education Program and Family Support Services.
PDF link

## [PDF page 6]
Resources Needed and Expenses:  
Aurora Organic Dairyoffered dairy workers $50 per vaccine dose to achieve high vaccination  
rates among staff. If a worker received a J&J/Janssen primary series, they received $50, and if a  
worker received a two shot primary series, Moderna or Pfizer, they received a total of $100. Dairy  
leadership required persistency in its efforts to promote vaccination clinics through flyers,  
meeting announcements, and Spanish text messages. If a worker had side effects from the  
vaccine, they could take the day off with pay and without any questions from dairy management.
Dr. Anabel Rodriguez and Dr. Douphrate of UTSPH provided culturally sensitive and linguistically  
appropriate COVID-19 education in paper flyers and audio pieces (English, Spanish, K’iche’).  
Through United Stated Department of Agriculture (USDA) funding, their research team created  
COVID-19 mitigation and prevention educational materials for dairy workers.
Twenty iPad tablets were available to dairy workers to create an asynchronous personal mobile-  
learning  experience  in  English,  Spanish,  or  K’iche’.  Funding  from  the  National  Center  for  
Farmworker Health (NCFH)Demonstration Grantalso supported their efforts to vaccinate dairy  
farm workers and their families.
Texas  DSHS  Public  Health  Region‘s  team  consisted  of  Melanie  Lee,  RN  (Clinical  
manager/director), four Texas DSHS registered nurses, four contract LVNs through the state of  
Texas, and six onsite data entry people from Lubbock, TX to help with consents and forms. The  
Preparedness and Response (PAR)team helped set up tarps and chairs, and Public Health Region  
1 Immunization Programassured all COVID-19 vaccines, Tdap, MMR, and influenza vaccines were  
onsite. Each onsite vaccination event required 22-23 individuals, including multiple volunteer  
interpreters/translators and individuals from local partnership organizations.
Partners:

· Family Support Servicesin Amarillo, TX  
·Texas RioGrande Legal Aid

**Texas Department of State Health Services** is a state agency of Texas. The department was created by House Bill 2292 of the 78th Texas Legislature in 2003 through the merging of four state agencies: the Texas Department of Health, Texas Department of Mental Health and Mental Retardation, Texas Health Care Information Council, and Texas Commission on Alcohol and Drug Abuse.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-1) The department provides state-operated health care services, including hospitals, health centers, and health agencies. The agency is headquartered at the Central Campus at 1100 West 49th Street in Austin.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-2) The DSHS Council governs the department.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-3)

The agency's Mental Health and Substance Abuse Division, along with Public Policy Research Institute at Texas A&M University coordinate the Texas School Survey,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-4) a program consisting of two surveys on drug and alcohol abuse, an annual one done at the local school-district level and a biennial statewide survey. The statewide survey, called the Texas School Survey of Substance Use, is the largest survey of its kind to be conducted in the United States and administered to over 100,000 public school students between grades 7–12.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-6)
Dr. Jennifer Shuford is the Commissioner of the Texas Department of State Health Services. She was appointed to this position in December 2022.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-7)

## Geographic structure
[edit]
The agency provides an array of public health services and oversight across the state through eight regional offices.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-10)

Texas Department of State Health Services

JurisdictionTexas

Parent agencyTexas Health and Human Services Commission
Austin State Hospital
**Texas Department of State Health Services** is a state agency of Texas. The department was created by House Bill 2292 of the 78th Texas Legislature in 2003 through the merging of four state agencies: the Texas Department of Health, Texas Department of Mental Health and Mental Retardation, Texas Health Care Information Council, and Texas Commission on Alcohol and Drug Abuse.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-1) The department provides state-operated health care services, including hospitals, health centers, and health agencies. The agency is headquartered at the Central Campus at 1100 West 49th Street in Austin.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-2) The DSHS Council governs the department.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-3)

The agency's Mental Health and Substance Abuse Division, along with Public Policy Research Institute at Texas A&M University coordinate the Texas School Survey,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-4) a program consisting of two surveys on drug and alcohol abuse, an annual one done at the local school-district level and a biennial statewide survey. The statewide survey, called the Texas School Survey of Substance Use, is the largest survey of its kind to be conducted in the United States and administered to over 100,000 public school students between grades 7–12.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-6)
Dr. Jennifer Shuford is the Commissioner of the Texas Department of State Health Services. She was appointed to this position in December 2022.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-7)

## Geographic structure
[edit]
The agency provides an array of public health services and oversight across the state through eight regional offices.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-10)
